label: Decca
rationale: New York, N.Y. is George Russell's orchestral demonstration of the Lydian Chromatic Concept of Tonal Organization, the harmony theory he worked out during a 1945-46 hospital stay and self-published in 1953 -- the same body of ideas Wikipedia credits as 'a crucial influence on John Coltrane and Miles Davis on the classic recording Kind of Blue' and 'a beacon for other modernists such as Eric Dolphy and Art Farmer' [S8] (obs). Lineage is the strongest signal here: the record is the large-ensemble statement of the theory that sits under the modal records already in this canon, and Russell is already present through Ezz-thetics (1961) [S3,S8] (inf). Session gravity is its second claim. Three sessions across 1958-59 -- September 12 and November 24, 1958, and March 25, 1959 -- each convened a different orchestra, and between them they pulled Bill Evans, John Coltrane, Max Roach, Art Farmer, Bob Brookmeyer, Phil Woods, Benny Golson, Al Cohn, Doc Severinsen, Barry Galbraith and Milt Hinton onto one record, with Coltrane, Evans and Roach together on the opening 'Manhattan' [S1,S2,S4] (obs). Standing: AllMusic rates it 4.5/5 and files it under Post-Bop, Ken Dryden writing that 'George Russell was one of the most forward-thinking composers and arrangers on the jazz scene during the 1950s' and that the album 'represents one of many high points in his career'; the Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide and Down Beat both give it 5/5 [S1,S3] (obs). The critical consensus is strong but not unanimous -- the Penguin Guide rates it 3/5 [S1] (obs). It still plays: 'Big City Blues' is an 11:40 Russell original, the East Side Medley folds 'Autumn in New York' and 'How About You' into a single eight-minute band, and Jon Hendricks's spoken narration links the performances [S1,S3,S4] (obs). Dating and release: recorded in New York City in 1958-59, issued July or August 1959 on Decca DL 9216, reissued on Impulse! in 1998 and by Decca/Verve in the 2021 Acoustic Sounds series [S1,S2,S4,S6] (obs). Place note: no source consulted names a studio -- AllMusic gives the recording location only as 'New York, NY' and the sessionography only as 'New York City' -- so each session carries the canon's city-level place rather than a named room [S2,S3,S4] (obs).

personnel_record.notes: Three Decca sessions, all in New York City with no studio named by any source consulted: September 12, 1958 (Manhattan), November 24, 1958 (Manhatta-Rico; A Helluva Town), March 25, 1959 (Big City Blues; East Side Medley). Session dates from the Art Farmer sessionography (S2) and the 2021 reissue's sleeve note 'Recorded in New York on Sept. 12, 1958 (A1), Nov. 24, 1958 (B1, B3), and March 25, 1959 (A2, B2)' (S4); both agree, and AllMusic gives the recording span as September 12, 1958 - March 25, 1959 (S3). Location: AllMusic gives only 'New York, NY' (S3), the sessionography only 'New York City' (S2), the reissue only 'Recorded in New York' (S4) -- hence the city-level canonical place for each session and no invented studio. Drummer split on the November 24 date: Max Roach plays 'A Helluva Town' and Don Lamond 'Manhatta-Rico' (S2), which the reissue credits match once its side assignment is read (Drums: Don Lamond B1, Max Roach B3, and Al Epstein's bongos on B1 fix B1 as Manhatta-Rico) (S4) -- recorded as corroboration, not a conflict. LP layout follows the 2021 reissue: A1 Manhattan, A2 Big City Blues, B1 Manhatta-Rico, B2a Autumn In New York / B2b How About You (a single band, 'East Side Medley'), B3 A Helluva Town (S4). Track-title variants: 'Manhatta-Rico' (S2, S4) is printed 'Manhattan: Rico' on the Wikipedia CD listing (S1); 'How About You' appears as 'How About You?' (S1). Matrix numbers: 105626, 105627, 105628, 105629, 106127 (S2); the Fresh Sound reissue documentation cites 105630 for the East Side Medley (not verified in full). Personnel conflicts: Benny Golson is named for the March 25, 1959 session by the sessionography and the reissue credits (S2, S4) but is absent from the Wikipedia personnel list, which is sourced to the Penguin Guide (S1) -- he is recorded with obs against S2/S4. Hal McKusick and Phil Woods are credited on alto saxophone with clarinet and flute doubling (S2); Brookmeyer's valve trombone (S1, S2) is listed simply as trombone on the reissue (S4); Al Epstein's bongos (S2, S4) and George Russell's chromatic drums (S2, S4) have no taxonomy entries and are recorded as percussion and drums. Production: no producer or engineer is named by any source consulted -- the reissue credits carry only sleeve notes (Burt Korall), the 2021 LP mastering (Ryan Smith, Sterling Sound) and the reissue supervisor (Chad Kassem) (S4) -- so producer/engineer are explicit nulls with epistemic_production unk. Composer attribution: Wikipedia prints the medley as (Vernon Duke, Ira Gershwin)/(Ralph Freed, Burton Lane) (S1), but Discogs credits 'Autumn In New York' to Vernon Duke alone and 'How About You' to Burton Lane and Ralph Freed (S4); Ira Gershwin is therefore not recorded as a composer. Release: Decca DL 9216 (mono) / DL 79216 (stereo), July or August 1959 (S1, S2, S4); MCA two-fer with Jazz in the Space Age 1973; Impulse! IMPD-278 1998; Decca/Verve Acoustic Sounds 2021 (S2, S4, S6).

ballot.case_for: The album is Russell’s large-ensemble statement of the Lydian Chromatic Concept, connecting directly to the modal lineage already represented by Coltrane and Davis; the dossier cites this influence through S8, though that source is Wikipedia. Its three sessions assemble an unusually deep cross-section of late-1950s modernists, including Coltrane, Evans, Roach, Farmer, Brookmeyer, and Woods, and the ratings cited in S1—5/5 from Down Beat and the Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide, 4.5/5 from AllMusic—show substantial critical standing.
ballot.case_against: The Penguin Guide’s 3/5 rating (S1) is meaningful dissent against the stronger American ratings, and raises a fair question about whether Russell’s large-ensemble concept is as compelling in execution as his more celebrated small-group work. Hendricks’s spoken narration may date the listening experience, and the dossier does not establish that the album functions as essential discovery listening rather than as an important historical document; Coltrane, meanwhile, appears on only one track.
ballot.recommendation: Treat it as a strong but contested candidate, giving its lineage and exceptional session roster serious weight while letting the listening experience decide whether it earns a place.
